artifact.recommendation: Choose logical replication with a brief write pause, validation, and traffic switch. Keep the source authoritative and rollback-ready until correctness checks pass.
reasoning: It is the only option directly compatible with the approved maximum of 10 minutes of write unavailability; the big-bang option requires 30 minutes.
The staging rehearsal's 42-second peak lag suggests replication can converge comfortably within the window if the team pauses writes and verifies zero lag before switching.
CDC row-count and checksum comparisons provide an explicit correctness gate, reducing the risk of silently losing committed writes.
Keeping the source authoritative through validation preserves the demonstrated 7-minute rollback path.
Dual-write would require correct changes across 19 write paths, including three that bypass the main repository layer, creating substantial omission and divergence risk.
considerations: Define hard go/no-go gates: replication healthy before the window, writes demonstrably blocked, source commit position captured, target caught up to that position, checksums and critical invariants passing, and connection routing verified.
Do not resume writes on the target until replication convergence and mandatory correctness checks complete.
Keep the source intact and prevent split-brain writes after switching; rollback procedures must specify how target-side writes are reconciled if rollback is needed after writes resume.
Assign the four engineers explicit roles for replication, application traffic/write controls, validation, and incident coordination.
Run a production-like cutover rehearsal and prepare automated commands, timing checkpoints, abort thresholds, and stakeholder communications.
assumptions: Logical replication supports all relevant tables, data types, schema changes, sequences or identity generators, and transaction semantics used by the service.
The 42-second staging lag result is reasonably representative of production peak write volume and transaction size.
Required correctness checks can finish inside the maintenance window, or writes can safely remain paused until they finish without exceeding 10 minutes.
Traffic can be switched atomically enough to prevent clients from writing to both databases.
The rollback drill's 7-minute result applies to the planned production topology while the source remains authoritative.
risks: Production replication lag or long-running transactions could exceed rehearsal results and consume the maintenance window.
Logical replication may omit unsupported objects, sequence state, DDL, or tables not included in publication configuration.
CDC row counts and checksums may miss application-level invariants or recent transactions if compared at inconsistent positions.
Rollback becomes materially harder after accepting writes on the target because reverse replication or reconciliation would be required.
With no overnight vendor support and only four engineers, operational complexity and fatigue could slow diagnosis.
A non-atomic write pause or traffic switch could cause split-brain writes or acknowledged writes landing on the wrong database.
evidence_needed: A production-load or production-shadow rehearsal showing lag distribution, catch-up time, and total write-pause duration below 10 minutes with margin.
A complete replication inventory covering tables, partitions, sequences, identity values, large objects, triggers, DDL behavior, and unsupported data types.
Proof that the write-block mechanism covers every write path and that traffic switching cannot leave stale writers connected.
Measured duration and consistency semantics of row-count, checksum, and application-invariant validation at the same replication position.
A tested rollback plan for both phases: before target writes resume and after target writes resume.
Capacity and performance validation for the target under production read/write load.

citations.claim: Logical replication showed 42 seconds of lag at peak synthetic load in staging.
Dual-write would span 19 write paths across six modules, with three bypassing the main repository layer.
Rollback completed in 7 minutes when the source remained authoritative.
A full export/import took 96 minutes, making it unsuitable for the cutover window.
The approved maintenance window permits at most 10 minutes of write unavailability.
CDC monitoring can compare source and target row counts and checksums during cutover.

artifact.recommendation: Choose logical replication with a brief write pause, validation, and traffic switch. Keep the source database authoritative and rollback-capable until correctness checks pass.
reasoning: This is the only option directly supported by a staging rehearsal while remaining compatible with the 10-minute write-unavailability cap.
The observed 42-second peak replication lag leaves substantial time within the approved window to pause writes, drain replication, verify synchronization, and switch traffic.
Keeping the source authoritative through validation preserves the demonstrated 7-minute rollback path and reduces the chance of losing committed writes.
A 30-minute big-bang freeze violates the approved 10-minute cap, while the 96-minute export/import rehearsal makes that approach operationally unsuitable.
Dual-write creates material correctness risk because writes span 19 paths across six modules, including three paths that bypass the main repository layer.
considerations: Define explicit gates: block writes, record the source position, wait for replication lag to reach zero, run CDC row-count/checksum checks, switch traffic, perform smoke tests, then declare the target authoritative.

Ensure the rollback decision is made early enough to complete the demonstrated 7-minute procedure within the maintenance window if that window constrains total operational activity, not only write unavailability.
Assign the four engineers distinct roles for command execution, validation, application/traffic control, and incident coordination.
Prevent target-side writes before the switch and source-side writes after the switch unless a tested reverse-replication or reconciliation mechanism exists.
Use predetermined abort thresholds for replication lag, checksum mismatch, error rate, and elapsed time.
assumptions: Logical replication supports every required table, data type, sequence, schema change, and write operation used by the service.
The 42-second staging lag is representative of peak production behavior.
The 10-minute constraint applies specifically to planned write unavailability, as stated.
CDC checks can finish quickly enough to support an initial correctness decision during the cutover.
Application writes can be reliably blocked and in-flight transactions can be drained.
risks: Production replication lag may exceed the staging result and consume the cutover budget.
Row counts and checksums may miss semantic errors or may take too long on the 1.8 TB table without incremental validation.
Sequences, generated values, large objects, DDL, triggers, or replication-excluded objects could diverge even when replicated rows match.
Once writes are accepted on the target, rolling back to a stale source could lose those newly committed writes; rollback safety therefore changes at that point.
With no overnight vendor support and only four engineers, an unexpected replication or database failure may exceed the team's operational capacity.
evidence_needed: A production-like load test demonstrating worst-case replication drain time and total write-pause duration below 10 minutes.
A complete replication-coverage audit for all tables, sequences, data types, DDL behavior, and non-table objects.
Measured runtimes and acceptance thresholds for CDC row-count/checksum validation, especially for the 1.8 TB table.
A production runbook rehearsal covering write fencing, in-flight transaction draining, traffic switching, and timed abort decisions.
A tested rollback design for the period after target writes begin, or an explicit point-of-no-return with product approval.
Confirmation that connection strings, background workers, batch jobs, and all 19 write paths obey the write pause and traffic switch.

citations.claim: Logical replication reached 42 seconds of lag at peak synthetic load in staging.
The application has 19 write paths across six modules, with three bypassing the main repository layer, increasing dual-write implementation risk.
Rollback to an authoritative source was rehearsed in 7 minutes.
A full export/import of the 1.8 TB largest table took 96 minutes in rehearsal.
The approved maintenance window caps write unavailability at 10 minutes.
CDC monitoring can compare source and target row counts and checksums during cutover.

strengths: The recommendation directly satisfies the stated write-unavailability constraint, unlike the 30-minute big-bang option.
It correctly identifies dual-write risk from the 19 distributed write paths, especially the three bypassing the repository layer.
It distinguishes rollback before and after target-side writes begin and explicitly recognizes the danger of losing writes committed only to the target.
The proposed gates, role assignments, abort thresholds, coverage audit, and production-like rehearsal are operationally relevant.
Claims are traceable to the supplied evidence, and major uncertainties are disclosed as assumptions or evidence gaps.
weaknesses: The report says the source should remain authoritative until correctness checks pass, but its runbook switches traffic before smoke tests and final validation; that sequence makes the target authoritative for new writes and undermines the stated rollback model.
It treats 42 seconds of staging lag as leaving “substantial time” in a 10-minute window without measured production drain time, transaction-drain time, validation runtime, or traffic-switch duration.

The 7-minute rollback result is presented as preserving a rollback path, although it was demonstrated only while the source remained authoritative and may leave too little time for detection and decision-making within a 10-minute write pause.
It does not define whether traffic switching includes reads only, writes, or both, making the authority transition and rollback semantics ambiguous.
It does not clearly separate rapid cutover checks from comprehensive validation that may be infeasible during the pause.
unsupported: The claim that logical replication is the only option directly supported by a staging rehearsal is too broad; the evidence also describes export/import and rollback rehearsals, although those do not make big-bang compliant.
The conclusion that 42 seconds leaves substantial cutover time is unsupported without timings for every other critical-path operation.
The assertion that keeping the source authoritative through validation preserves the demonstrated rollback path is unsupported if target writes are enabled before validation completes.
The report implicitly treats CDC row counts and checksums as usable within the cutover window, but no runtime or scalability evidence is provided for the 1.8 TB table.
missing: A precise timeline allocating the 10-minute write-pause budget across fencing, draining transactions, catching up replication, validation, switching, smoke testing, abort decision, and recovery.
A write-authority state machine showing when source writes stop, when target writes begin, and exactly when rollback ceases to be lossless.
A concrete rollback mechanism after target writes begin, such as tested reverse replication, durable write capture and replay, or a formally approved point of no return.
Verification that logical replication preserves transaction ordering, referential integrity, sequences or identities, large objects, triggers, and schema compatibility for this specific system.
A validation design that distinguishes fast blocking checks from slower post-cutover checks and defines mismatch handling.
Operational provisions for alerting, backups or recovery points, credentials, capacity, replication-slot growth, long-running transactions, and background or external writers.
Clear scheduling relative to available staffing and the absence of overnight vendor support.
incorrect_assumptions: It assumes staging synthetic peak load is representative of production despite identifying that assumption as unverified.
It assumes all application and non-application writers can be reliably fenced, despite three write paths bypassing the main repository layer and no evidence about jobs or external clients.
It assumes the demonstrated 7-minute rollback remains applicable to the recommended traffic-switch sequence; that drill applies only while the source remains authoritative.
It appears to assume validation can occur before target authority changes while simultaneously placing smoke tests after the traffic switch.
critical_risks: Enabling target writes before correctness approval can make a rollback to the source silently discard committed target-only writes, violating a hard constraint.
An unmeasured validation or replication-drain duration could exceed the 10-minute write-unavailability limit and force a rushed, ambiguous abort decision.
Incomplete logical-replication coverage could produce divergence that row counts and basic checksums do not detect.
Failure to fence every writer could create split-brain writes across source and target.
The four-person team may be unable to execute cutover, validation, rollback, and incident response safely during an unexpected failure without vendor support.
recommended_changes: Make the authority transition explicit: keep all writes fenced while replication drains and blocking checks run, then either commit irreversibly to the target or enable a tested mechanism that captures target writes for lossless rollback.
Replace “substantial time” with a measured cutover budget and require a production-scale rehearsal demonstrating margin below 10 minutes.
Define separate pre-switch blocking checks and post-switch non-blocking checks, with exact thresholds and actions for mismatches.
Specify a timed decision deadline that accounts for detection plus the seven-minute rollback, rather than merely noting that rollback must begin early.
Treat the first target write as the point of no return unless reverse replication or replay has been tested; obtain explicit product approval for that boundary.
Audit and test fencing for every application path, worker, batch process, administrative client, and external integration.
Lower the stated confidence until production-representative lag, validation timing, replication coverage, and post-switch rollback are demonstrated.

strengths: The recommendation directly compares all three options against the stated constraints and correctly rejects the 30-minute big-bang freeze as incompatible with the 10-minute cap.
It identifies the unusually high implementation risk of dual-write across 19 write paths, especially the three paths bypassing the repository layer.
It uses the supplied evidence accurately and maintains clear traceability through artifact locators.
The proposed go/no-go gates address replication health, write blocking, commit-position capture, convergence, validation, and routing.
It recognizes split-brain, unsupported replication objects, inconsistent validation snapshots, long-running transactions, and post-switch rollback as major hazards.
Explicit roles, automation, abort thresholds, rehearsal, and stakeholder communications are appropriate controls for a four-engineer team without overnight vendor support.
The evidence-needed section is strong and appropriately calls for replication inventory, write-path coverage, validation timing, rollback testing, and target capacity testing.
weaknesses: The recommendation is more confident than the available evidence warrants; several prerequisites that determine basic feasibility remain unverified.
The phrase "converge comfortably within the window" overstates what one staging result under synthetic load establishes and does not account for total pause, validation, routing, or abort time.
The report does not present a concrete minute-by-minute cutover budget or specify how much safety margin is required below 10 minutes.

The authority and rollback sequence is not completely precise: it should explicitly distinguish source-authoritative replication, validation, read switch, target write enablement, and the point at which simple rollback ceases to be available.
It does not define which correctness checks are mandatory before writes resume versus which checks may safely continue afterward.
It mentions long-running transactions but does not specify a pre-cutover drain, termination policy, or abort threshold for them.
unsupported: The claim that 42 seconds of staging lag implies comfortable convergence within the maintenance window is unsupported without production-representative throughput, transaction-size, contention, and catch-up measurements.

The claim that CDC row counts and checksums reduce silent-write-loss risk is directionally reasonable, but their adequacy is unsupported until consistent-position semantics, coverage, collision properties, and execution duration are established.
The production applicability of the seven-minute rollback drill is unproven for the intended topology and operational conditions.
Feasibility of completing replication convergence, correctness validation, routing changes, and any necessary abort within the 10-minute write-unavailability limit is not demonstrated.
Atomic or sufficiently coordinated blocking of every writer and traffic switching is not demonstrated.
missing: A precise state machine naming the authoritative database and permitted write destinations at every cutover and rollback phase.
An end-to-end timing budget covering write drain, final catch-up, commit-position verification, mandatory validation, connection termination, routing, smoke tests, and rollback decision time.
A clear interpretation of the requirement that rollback remain possible until correctness checks complete, including whether target writes may begin before all such checks finish.
Explicit success, abort, and rollback thresholds, including maximum lag, validation duration, error rate, and remaining-window margin.
A plan for existing connection pools, background workers, scheduled jobs, retries, queues, and clients that may retain stale source connections.
Verification of replication slots, WAL retention, storage headroom, replication failure recovery, and behavior during network interruption.
Sequence or identity synchronization and verification immediately before enabling target writes.
Schema-freeze and DDL-handling procedures during replication and cutover.
A reconciliation or reverse-replication design if rollback must remain possible after target writes are accepted.
Recovery objectives and procedures for a partial switch, including acknowledged writes reaching both databases.

A decision on whether full-table checksums for the 1.8 TB table are operationally feasible within the window, plus scoped alternatives such as position-aligned incremental checks and application invariants.
incorrect_assumptions: It implicitly treats peak synthetic load as a reasonable proxy for production without evidence about workload fidelity.

It implicitly assumes that the seven-minute rollback leaves enough time within the same 10-minute outage constraint; the constraint applies to write unavailability, so rollback timing must be included in the failure-path budget.
It assumes required validation can fit within the window, although no validation duration is provided and the largest table is 1.8 TB.
It assumes all writers can be blocked and traffic switched coherently despite evidence that some write paths bypass the main repository layer.
It assumes keeping the source intact is sufficient for rollback; once target writes resume, source intactness alone does not preserve a lossless rollback path.
critical_risks: A failed or slow cutover may exceed the approved 10-minute write-unavailability cap because the report has not shown an end-to-end success or rollback timing budget.
If target writes begin before correctness checks complete, rollback could lose or require reconciliation of committed target-side writes, violating the no-silent-loss constraint.
A stale application instance, worker, or connection pool could continue writing to the source after target writes begin, producing split-brain state.
Logical replication coverage gaps involving tables, partitions, sequences, DDL, large objects, or unsupported types could pass superficial row-count checks while leaving the target incorrect.
Checks performed at different replication positions could produce misleading results or fail to detect missing recent transactions.
Insufficient WAL retention, slot failure, storage exhaustion, or an unhandled long-running transaction could prevent final convergence during the window.
recommended_changes: Make the recommendation conditional: select logical replication only after production-like rehearsal and replication-inventory gates prove the complete cutover and rollback paths fit below 10 minutes with explicit margin.
Replace "converge comfortably" with a narrower statement that the 42-second rehearsal is encouraging but insufficient to establish production timing.
Add a minute-by-minute success-path and failure-path budget, reserving time for abort and the demonstrated seven-minute rollback where applicable.
Define an explicit authority sequence, preferably keeping source writes authoritative and target writes disabled until mandatory checks complete, then performing a controlled final switch.
State exactly when rollback changes from simple routing back to requiring reverse replication or reconciliation, and test both cases if rollback must remain available after target writes begin.
Specify mandatory pre-resume checks based on a captured source commit position, including replication-position equality, sequence state, critical-table checks, and application invariants.
Prove write fencing across all application instances, bypass paths, workers, queues, jobs, administrative tools, and retained database connections.
Add operational controls for transaction draining, schema freeze, WAL and slot monitoring, storage headroom, sequence synchronization, and stale-connection termination.
Lower the report confidence until the identified feasibility evidence is obtained.

attacks: The recommendation is not presently proven feasible; it should be conditional on production-scale timing, replication-coverage, and write-fencing gates rather than selected outright.

The 42-second staging lag measures only one component under synthetic load. It does not justify claims of comfortable margin within a 10-minute budget that must also cover transaction drain, final catch-up, validation, routing, smoke tests, abort detection, and recovery.

The proposed authority model is internally inconsistent: keeping the source authoritative until checks pass conflicts with switching traffic or enabling target writes before final validation. Once the target accepts writes, routing back to the source is no longer a lossless rollback.

The demonstrated seven-minute rollback leaves at most three minutes for failure detection and decision-making if rollback occurs during the same write outage, making the failure path implausibly tight.
CDC row counts and checksums are being treated as a correctness gate without evidence that they are position-consistent, sufficiently comprehensive, or fast enough for a 1.8 TB table.
Keeping the source intact is incorrectly conflated with preserving rollback. It preserves simple rollback only while no committed target-only writes exist.
Logical replication can omit sequences, DDL, large objects, triggers, partitions, or unsupported operations while superficial row checks still pass.
Dual-write is rightly risky, but rejecting it does not establish that logical replication satisfies the hard constraints; all options may currently be infeasible.

Four engineers without overnight vendor support may be insufficient for simultaneous database control, application fencing, validation, routing, and incident response, especially if the cutover encounters an untested production failure.
falsifiers: A production-like end-to-end rehearsal exceeds 10 minutes on either the success path or a realistic abort-and-rollback path.
Any table, partition, data type, sequence, identity, large object, trigger-dependent effect, or transaction pattern cannot be reproduced correctly by the logical-replication setup.

A full writer-fencing test shows that any application instance, bypass path, worker, job, queue consumer, administrative client, retry, or stale connection can still commit to the source after the switch.
Mandatory position-aligned validation cannot complete with required safety margin before writes must resume.
Production-tail replication lag, long-running transactions, WAL volume, or slot behavior materially exceeds the staging synthetic result.
Rollback after the first target write cannot preserve or reconcile every acknowledged target-side commit.
Traffic-switch fault injection produces simultaneous source and target writes, dropped acknowledged writes, or ambiguous commit outcomes.
Sequence or identity synchronization permits duplicate keys or value regression after target write enablement.
Target production-load testing reveals inadequate latency, throughput, storage, or connection capacity.
evidence_gaps: A minute-by-minute success-path budget with explicit safety margin below the 10-minute write-unavailability cap.
A failure-path budget covering detection, decision, abort, and the seven-minute rollback—not merely rollback execution.
A precise authority state machine identifying allowed write destinations, validation gates, and the exact point at which simple rollback ceases to be lossless.
A production-representative lag distribution and final drain time, including peak transaction sizes, long-running transactions, contention, and network degradation.
Measured duration and consistency semantics for mandatory checks, especially on the 1.8 TB table, plus a separation between blocking and post-cutover validation.
A complete replication inventory covering all database objects and application semantics, including sequences, identities, DDL, partitions, large objects, triggers, and unsupported operations.
Proof that every writer and retained connection can be fenced and redirected coherently across all 19 write paths and non-application clients.
A tested mechanism for lossless rollback after target writes begin, or explicit approval that the first target write is a point of no return.
Evidence for WAL retention, replication-slot resilience, storage headroom, schema freeze, network-failure recovery, backups, and target capacity.
A staffed execution schedule and contingency model appropriate for four engineers and absent overnight vendor support.

accepted_criticisms: The recommendation should be conditional because production feasibility has not been demonstrated through an end-to-end rehearsal, replication inventory, and comprehensive write-fencing test.

The 42-second staging lag is encouraging but does not establish comfortable margin within the 10-minute limit; it excludes drain, catch-up, validation, routing, smoke testing, failure detection, and recovery.
No success-path or failure-path timing budget demonstrates compliance with the 10-minute write-unavailability cap, especially given the seven-minute rollback drill.
CDC row counts and checksums are not yet proven position-consistent, comprehensive, collision-appropriate, or fast enough for mandatory validation, particularly with a 1.8 TB table.
Keeping the source intact preserves simple lossless rollback only until the target accepts committed writes; later rollback requires tested reverse replication or reconciliation.
Logical replication coverage remains unproven for sequences, identities, DDL, partitions, large objects, triggers, unsupported operations, and application semantics.
Rejecting big-bang and dual-write does not itself prove logical replication feasible; all listed options may currently fail the constraints.
The report needs a precise authority state machine, mandatory pre-resume checks, explicit abort thresholds, transaction-drain controls, and proof that all writers and stale connections can be fenced.
Confidence of 0.93 was too high given that basic feasibility gates remain open.
rejected_criticisms: The proposed authority model is not inherently inconsistent: the report explicitly says not to resume target writes until convergence and mandatory correctness checks complete. Its actual defect is insufficiently precise sequencing and an unresolved rollback requirement after target writes begin.

The evidence does not establish that four engineers are insufficient. Staffing is a material operational risk requiring rehearsal and role planning, but insufficiency cannot be concluded from the visible evidence alone.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Do not yet approve any option for production execution. Treat logical replication as the leading candidate, but select it only after production-like end-to-end success and abort rehearsals demonstrate write unavailability below 10 minutes with explicit margin; replication coverage and position-aligned validation are proven; every writer is fenced; and rollback remains lossless until required correctness checks finish. If those gates cannot be met, escalate because none of the current options satisfies all constraints.
reasons: Big-bang directly violates the approved 10-minute cap, while dual-write carries substantial unproven risk across 19 write paths, including three bypass paths.
Logical replication is therefore the strongest candidate, but candidate superiority is not proof of constraint satisfaction.
The sole timing result covers only staging replication lag and cannot establish the complete production outage duration.

The demonstrated rollback is seven minutes only while the source remains authoritative, leaving little failure-detection and decision time and providing no evidence for lossless rollback after target writes.
The visible evidence does not establish replication completeness, writer fencing, validation duration or semantics, target capacity, or a safe authority transition.

accepted_criticisms: The recommendation was too definitive; logical replication should be selected only after production-scale timing, replication-coverage, validation, and writer-fencing gates pass.

The 42-second staging lag does not establish adequate margin within the 10-minute write-unavailability budget because transaction drain, final catch-up, blocking validation, switching, failure detection, and abort timing are unmeasured.
The authority model and runbook were inconsistent: switching writes to the target before correctness approval defeats the claim that the source remains authoritative and simply rollback-capable.
The seven-minute rollback drill applies only while the source remains authoritative and leaves very little time for detection and decision if the entire failure path must fit within the write outage.
CDC row counts and checksums were treated as practical blocking checks without evidence of position consistency, coverage, or runtime for the 1.8 TB table.
Keeping the source intact preserves lossless rollback only until the first acknowledged target-only write.
Logical-replication coverage for sequences, identities, DDL, large objects, triggers, partitions, transaction semantics, and unsupported operations is unproven.
Rejecting big-bang and dual-write does not itself prove logical replication feasible; the visible evidence permits the conclusion that none of the options is currently ready.
The four-engineer staffing model may be inadequate for cutover control, fencing, validation, routing, rollback, and incident response without vendor support.
The report needed separate fast blocking checks from comprehensive post-cutover validation and a precise write-authority state machine.

The claim that logical replication was the only option directly supported by rehearsal was imprecise because export/import and rollback rehearsals were also documented, even though they do not establish another compliant option.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Do not approve any option unconditionally yet. Treat logical replication as the leading candidate, but authorize it only after a production-representative end-to-end rehearsal proves a safely bounded sub-10-minute write pause; complete replication-object and semantic coverage; position-aligned blocking checks with measured runtimes; comprehensive writer fencing; and an explicit authority state machine. Keep writes fenced while draining replication and running blocking checks. Unless tested reverse replication or durable replay exists, define the first target write as an approved point of no return rather than claiming rollback remains lossless afterward. If these gates fail, escalate because the other listed options also do not satisfy the current constraints.
reasons: Big-bang directly violates the 10-minute cap, and dual-write across 19 dispersed paths presents substantial split-brain and omission risk, so logical replication remains the strongest candidate.
The visible evidence does not prove that logical replication can complete all critical-path operations within 10 minutes; 42 seconds measures only staging replication lag.
The only demonstrated seven-minute rollback assumes continued source authority and therefore does not cover rollback after target writes begin.
No evidence establishes complete logical-replication semantics, universal writer fencing, scalable validation, or sufficient production staffing.
Because silent loss of committed writes is prohibited, authority transition and rollback semantics must be proven before approval, not left as assumptions.

artifact.decision: Do not approve any option for production execution yet. Logical replication is the leading candidate, but it is acceptable only after production-representative timing, replication-coverage, position-aligned validation, comprehensive writer-fencing, and rollback-authority gates pass.
artifact.action: Require an end-to-end success and abort rehearsal with explicit sub-10-minute budgets and safety margin; audit replication semantics and every writer; measure blocking validation; and define a precise authority state machine in which writes remain fenced until mandatory checks pass. Treat the first target write as the point of no return unless tested reverse replication or durable replay preserves every acknowledged commit.
reasons: The 30-minute big-bang freeze directly violates the 10-minute write-unavailability cap.
Dual-write is especially hazardous across 19 write paths in six modules, including three bypass paths, but its weakness does not prove logical replication feasible.

The 42-second staging lag measures only replication lag under synthetic load, not the complete production critical path of transaction drain, catch-up, validation, routing, smoke testing, failure detection, and abort.

The seven-minute rollback was demonstrated only while the source remained authoritative; it does not establish lossless rollback after target-side writes begin and leaves little failure-detection margin if rollback shares the outage budget.
CDC row counts and checksums are available, but their consistent-position semantics, completeness, and runtime—especially against a 1.8 TB table—are not established.
The hard requirements of no silent committed-write loss and rollback until correctness checks complete require proven write authority and fencing, not merely retaining the source database.
evidence: Evidence e5 caps planned write unavailability at 10 minutes, while the big-bang option requires a 30-minute freeze.
Evidence e2 identifies 19 write paths across six modules, with three bypassing the main repository layer.
Evidence e1 reports 42 seconds of lag only in a staging rehearsal at peak synthetic load.
Evidence e3 reports a seven-minute rollback specifically when the source remained authoritative.
Evidence e4 reports a 1.8 TB largest production table and a 96-minute full export/import rehearsal.
Evidence e6 states only that CDC monitoring can compare row counts and checksums; it gives no validation duration or consistency guarantees.
The problem context explicitly requires rollback to remain possible until correctness checks complete.
rejected_alternatives: Reject unconditional logical-replication approval because complete timing and correctness feasibility remain unproven.
Reject big-bang because its specified 30-minute freeze exceeds the approved 10-minute cap.
Reject dual-write as currently unproven and operationally risky across numerous dispersed and bypassing write paths.
Reject the inference that keeping the source intact alone guarantees rollback after acknowledged target-only writes.
Reject treating the 42-second staging lag as evidence of comfortable end-to-end timing margin.
minority: The visible evidence does not prove that four engineers are categorically insufficient; staffing is a serious operational risk that should be tested through role-based rehearsal.
Logical replication remains the strongest candidate despite not yet being approvable.

A point-of-no-return after mandatory checks may satisfy the rollback requirement without reverse replication, provided correctness checks are complete before the first target write and the boundary is explicitly approved.
unresolved: Whether all tables, partitions, data types, sequences, identities, large objects, triggers, DDL effects, and transaction semantics replicate correctly.
Whether every application instance, bypass path, worker, queue consumer, scheduled job, administrative client, retry, and stale connection can be fenced.
The measured duration and source-position consistency of mandatory blocking validation.
Production-tail lag, long-running transaction behavior, WAL retention, slot resilience, storage headroom, and target capacity.
Whether both the success path and realistic detection-plus-abort path remain below 10 minutes with safety margin.
The exact meaning of rollback availability if any correctness checks continue after target writes resume.
assumptions: The 10-minute limit applies to total continuous planned write unavailability, including failed-cutover recovery while writes remain unavailable.
No reverse replication, durable target-write replay, or equivalent reconciliation mechanism has been demonstrated.
The 96-minute export/import rehearsal is relevant evidence against bulk-copy cutover, but the artifact does not explicitly state that the rehearsal was solely for the 1.8 TB table.
Mandatory correctness checks must finish before target writes begin if simple lossless rollback to the source is required until those checks complete.
change_conditions: Approve logical replication if a production-representative rehearsal proves complete success and realistic abort paths below 10 minutes with explicit margin.
Approve only after replication inventory and semantic tests cover every relevant object and operation.
Approve only after position-aligned blocking checks have measured runtimes and acceptance thresholds compatible with the outage budget.
Approve only after comprehensive fencing and traffic-switch fault injection show no split-brain, lost acknowledged writes, or ambiguous commits.

Permit rollback after target writes only if tested reverse replication or durable replay preserves every acknowledged target commit; otherwise approve the first target write as the post-validation point of no return.
Escalate for a changed constraint, redesigned option, or additional maintenance window if these gates cannot pass.
next_validation: Run a production-scale end-to-end rehearsal and record a minute-by-minute success-path budget.
Inject late failures and measure detection, decision, abort, seven-minute rollback, and total write-unavailability time.
Build and test a complete replication-object and application-semantics inventory.
Capture a source commit position and benchmark position-aligned blocking checks, critical invariants, and sequence synchronization.
Exercise fencing across all 19 write paths plus background, administrative, retry, queue, and retained-connection paths.
Fault-inject routing and connection-pool transitions to test for simultaneous writes and ambiguous outcomes.
Load-test target capacity and test WAL, replication-slot, storage, schema-freeze, and network-failure behavior.

artifact.decision: Do not approve any option for production yet. Logical replication is the leading candidate, but approval must remain conditional on production-representative timing, complete replication coverage, position-aligned validation, comprehensive writer fencing, and a rollback/authority design that satisfies the no-silent-loss requirement.
artifact.action: Require end-to-end success-path and abort-path rehearsals with explicit sub-10-minute budgets and safety margin. Keep all writes fenced during final catch-up and mandatory checks. Do not enable target writes until those checks pass; unless tested reverse replication or durable replay exists, formally treat the first target write as the point of no return. Escalate if these gates fail because neither alternative currently satisfies all constraints.
reasons: The 30-minute big-bang freeze directly violates the approved 10-minute write-unavailability cap.
Dual-write is exceptionally risky across 19 write paths, including three bypassing the main repository layer, and has no demonstrated mechanism preventing omissions or divergence.

The 42-second staging result measures replication lag under synthetic load, not the full production critical path of fencing, transaction drain, catch-up, validation, routing, smoke testing, abort detection, and recovery.
The seven-minute rollback was demonstrated only while the source remained authoritative; it does not prove lossless rollback after target-only writes begin.
CDC row counts and checksums are available, but their position consistency, coverage, and runtime—especially against a 1.8 TB table—are not established.

The requirement that rollback remain possible until correctness checks complete requires an explicit authority state machine. Enabling target writes before those checks finish would make simple rollback potentially lose acknowledged writes.
Logical replication is the strongest candidate by elimination and available rehearsal evidence, but its compliance with the hard constraints is not yet proven.
evidence: Problem e1: staging logical replication reached 42 seconds of lag at peak synthetic load.
Problem e2: the application has 19 write paths across six modules, with three bypassing the main repository layer.
Problem e3: rollback took seven minutes when the source remained authoritative.
Problem e4: the largest production table is 1.8 TB, and full export/import rehearsal took 96 minutes.
Problem e5: the approved maintenance window caps write unavailability at 10 minutes.
Problem e6: CDC monitoring can compare source and target row counts and checksums during cutover, but no timing or consistency guarantees are supplied.
Both rebuttals converge on conditional approval only after timing, coverage, validation, fencing, and rollback gates; this conclusion is independently supported by the problem evidence.
rejected_alternatives: Reject unconditional logical-replication approval because the visible evidence does not prove end-to-end feasibility or rollback safety.
Reject big-bang because its specified 30-minute freeze exceeds the hard 10-minute cap; the 96-minute export/import rehearsal further weakens its operational suitability.
Reject dual-write as presently unproven because safely modifying and coordinating all 19 write paths would introduce substantial split-brain, omission, and reconciliation risk.
Reject the claim that keeping the source intact alone preserves rollback after target writes begin; it does not preserve acknowledged target-only commits.
Reject treating row counts and checksums alone as a sufficient correctness gate without position alignment, measured runtime, and semantic coverage.
minority: A logical-replication cutover could be feasible if mandatory checks are narrowly scoped and precomputed, but the artifacts contain no measurements proving this.
The evidence does not prove that four engineers are categorically insufficient; staffing is a significant operational risk that should be tested through role-based rehearsal.
The 10-minute constraint explicitly concerns write unavailability, not total maintenance activity, but any rollback performed while writes remain unavailable still consumes that budget.
unresolved: Whether all tables, partitions, data types, sequences, identities, large objects, triggers, DDL effects, and transaction semantics are correctly replicated.
Whether every application instance, bypass path, worker, queue consumer, scheduled job, administrative client, retry, and stale connection can be fenced.
The complete success-path duration and required safety margin below 10 minutes.
The failure-path duration including detection, decision, abort, and seven-minute rollback.
The consistency semantics, coverage, and runtime of mandatory validation on production-scale data.
How acknowledged target-side writes would be preserved or reconciled if rollback is required after target write enablement.
Production-tail lag, long-running transaction behavior, WAL retention, slot resilience, storage headroom, network-failure handling, and target capacity.
Whether the four-engineer team can execute all roles safely without overnight vendor support.
assumptions: The listed options are the only options currently under consideration.
The 10-minute limit is a hard cap on continuous planned write unavailability.
No silent loss means every acknowledged commit must survive or be explicitly reconciled across all success and rollback paths.
Correctness checks referred to by the rollback requirement include at least the mandatory blocking checks needed before target writes resume.
No tested reverse-replication or durable target-write replay mechanism exists because none is evidenced in the artifacts.
change_conditions: Approve logical replication if production-representative success and realistic abort rehearsals both satisfy the write-unavailability cap with explicit margin.
Approve only after a complete replication inventory and semantic test show no unsupported or divergent database behavior.
Approve only after position-aligned blocking validation has measured runtimes and acceptance thresholds compatible with the outage budget.
Approve only after comprehensive fencing tests prove that no source writer remains after authority changes.
Approve only after the authority state machine preserves lossless rollback until required checks complete, either by delaying target writes or using tested reverse replication/replay.
Reconsider dual-write only if all 19 paths and non-application writers can be instrumented, audited, and reconciled with production-grade guarantees.
Reconsider big-bang only if its required write freeze is demonstrated below 10 minutes or the product formally changes the constraint.
next_validation: Create minute-by-minute success and failure budgets, including a fixed abort deadline that leaves enough time for rollback.
Run production-shadow or equivalent load tests covering peak WAL volume, long transactions, contention, degraded networking, and replication-slot behavior.
Audit replication coverage and test sequences, identities, partitions, DDL, triggers, large objects, unsupported types, and transaction ordering.
Measure position-aligned critical checks and application invariants on production-scale data; separate blocking checks from post-cutover validation.
Fault-inject traffic switching and stale connections while testing every application and non-application writer fence.
Test rollback both before target write enablement and after it using reverse replication or durable capture/replay; otherwise obtain approval for an explicit point of no return.
Load-test target performance, connections, storage, backups, WAL headroom, and recovery procedures.
Conduct a four-person role rehearsal with communications, command automation, handoffs, and incident scenarios.
